Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Financial Advisors and Retirees' Risk-taking
Allison T. Cole, Maarten Meeuwis, Alessandro Previtero, and Noah Stoffman
NBER Working Paper No. 35990
November 2026
JEL No. D15, G11, G24, G51, J26
ABSTRACT
Advised retirees keep about two-thirds of their portfolios in equities well into old age—30 to 40 
percentage points more than non-advised retirees, target-date funds, or common rules of thumb. 
These allocations reflect active choices rather than inertia, and they adjust gradually toward a new 
advisor’s investment style following advisor switches. Equity shares rise with relationship tenure, 
and advisor influence is strongest among clients with low financial knowledge or risk tolerance, 
consistent with trust facilitating risk-taking. Given retirees’ modest financial wealth relative to their 
safe pension income, we rationalize these portfolios in a standard life-cycle model with moderate 
risk aversion. Modeling advisors as “money doctors” who correct clients’ pessimistic beliefs about 
the equity premium, we find that, relative to a no-advice counterfactual, the welfare gains from 
higher risk-taking are of the same order of magnitude as the cost of advice.

Arizona State University

Introduction
About 68 percent of all U.S. retirement assets are invested in individual accounts, such as
IRAs and employer-sponsored defined contribution (DC) plans (Investment Company Insti-
tute, 2026). Retirees who rely on these accounts must manage their own savings throughout
retirement, deciding how much to withdraw each year and how much to keep invested in
stocks and bonds. This is a complex problem: the answer depends, among other things, on
expected asset returns and risks, longevity, medical expenses, and bequest motives. More-
over, retirees often face this problem amid declining cognitive abilities. 1 Not surprisingly,
many investors turn to financial advisors as retirement approaches: the use of financial ad-
visors peaks around age 65, when more than half of households with investable wealth rely
on professional investment advice (Figure 1). 2 Yet despite the prevalence of financial advice
in retirement, how advisors shape retirees’ portfolio decisions remains largely unexplored.
This paper studies the equity allocations of advised retirees and asks whether they are
sensible. Using administrative data on more than 36,000 advised Canadian retirees, we
document a novel fact: these retirees keep about two-thirds of their portfolios in equities
well into old age, much more than non-advised retirees, target-date fund glide paths, or
common industry rules of thumb. Advisors drive these allocations and hold equally risky
portfolios themselves, even after they stop advising clients. Clients’ willingness to follow this
advice is consistent with trust facilitating risk-taking. We show that the resulting allocations
are rationalized by a standard life-cycle model with moderate risk aversion. If advisors raise
risk-taking by correcting clients’ pessimistic beliefs about stock returns, the welfare gains
cover a substantial part of advisory fees.
We begin by estimating the age profile of the equity share of advised retirees. Because
age, cohort, and time effects cannot be separately identified without additional restrictions
1Older investors are more likely to make suboptimal financial (Agarwal, Driscoll, Gabaix, and Laibson,
2009) and investment decisions (Korniotis and Kumar, 2011; Ameriks, Caplin, Lee, Shapiro, and Tonetti,
2023) and more vulnerable to financial fraud (DeLiema, Deevy, Lusardi, and Mitchell, 2018).
2Figure 1 uses data from the U.S. Survey of Consumer Finances. In Canada, the 2019 Canadian Financial
Capability Survey estimates that 51% of investors 65 or older use financial advice.
1
(Ameriks and Zeldes, 2004), we follow Fagereng, Gottlieb, and Guiso (2017) and adopt the
approach of Deaton and Paxson (1994b). Advised retirees hold high equity shares well into
old age: the equity share declines from about 75 percent at age 65 to 55 percent at age 85.
These equity shares are 30 to 40 percentage points higher than those implied by the popular
“100 − age” rule and the glide path of the largest Canadian target-date fund family. The gap
is similar relative to non-advised Canadian retirees, whose equity shares of 25 to 30 percent
are in line with those documented in other countries (e.g., Fagereng et al., 2017).
These high equity shares reflect active portfolio choices rather than inertia. Retirees who
turn over more than a quarter of their portfolio in a given year hold nearly the same equity
shares as the full sample, and the equity share of new purchases declines from about 70
percent at age 65 to 50 percent at age 85. Assets held outside the advised accounts are also
unlikely to drive our results: when retirees receive large inflows into their advised accounts,
they invest the new money much like their existing portfolio, and their equity share falls by
only 2 percentage points on average.
We then ask what explains the variation in equity shares across retirees. One might
expect advisor effects to be weaker in retirement than in accumulation accounts, where
advisors strongly influence their clients’ equity shares (Foerster, Linnainmaa, Melzer, and
Previtero, 2017). Once labor income stops, optimal portfolios depend more heavily on clients’
preferences and circumstances, such as health, longevity, and bequest motives (e.g., Cocco,
Gomes, and Maenhout, 2005; Yogo, 2016; Lockwood, 2018), leaving less room for advisors’
own views.3 Yet investor characteristics explain little of this variation: gender, language, net
worth, and self-reported risk tolerance and financial knowledge together account for only 16
percent of it. In contrast, advisor identity matters much more. Adding advisor fixed effects
raises the adjusted R2 from 16 to 36 percent, and moving across the interquartile range of
advisors corresponds to a 15-percentage-point difference in equity share. Advisor effects thus
remain important in retirement.
3In Section 2.2, we discuss more extensively the theoretical and practical reasons why results observed
in accumulation accounts may not continue to hold in retirement.
2
This common variation among clients of the same advisor could reflect either advisors’
influence or the matching of investors with advisors who share their preferences. Following
Foerster et al. (2017), we distinguish between these explanations using investors who switch
advisors. After a switch, retirees’ equity shares gradually converge toward those of the
new advisor’s other clients, closing 28 percent of the gap between the new and the old
advisor within two years. We find a similar gradual convergence for investors whose switch
is involuntary because their advisor retires, dies, or leaves the industry, with no differential
trends before the switch. This evidence indicates that advisors directly influence their clients’
risk-taking and, together with the large gap between advised and non-advised portfolios, is
consistent with advice leading retirees to take substantially more risk. 4
Why do advisors steer their clients toward equities? One explanation is conflicts of
interest. Advisors are compensated through commissions and kickbacks, which can lead to
misselling and misconduct (Egan, Matvos, and Seru, 2019; Egan, Ge, and Tang, 2022), and
equity funds charge higher fees: in our data, a 10 percentage point higher equity share is
associated with a 7 basis point higher annual fee. These conflicts may be particularly strong
in retirement. Advisors’ commissions shrink as retirees draw down their assets, increasing
the incentive to invest the remaining wealth in higher-fee equity funds. Moreover, older
clients may be less able to monitor their accounts. In fact, advisor misconduct is more
common in counties with older populations (Egan et al., 2019). Alternatively, advisors may
recommend high equity shares because they sincerely believe that these allocations benefit
their clients. To distinguish between these explanations, we follow Foerster et al. (2017) and
Linnainmaa, Melzer, and Previtero (2021) and compare advisors’ own portfolios with those
of their clients, focusing on advisors who are themselves of retirement age. These advisors
hold equity shares that are statistically indistinguishable from those of their own clients,
even after they have stopped advising clients and no longer have career incentives to hold
4Using a regulatory change implemented in a staggered fashion across Canada, Linnainmaa, Melzer,
Previtero, and Foerster (2025) document a causal effect of financial advisors on clients’ stock market partic-
ipation.
3
similar portfolios. As in accumulation accounts, the high equity shares of advised retirees
thus appear to reflect advisors’ sincerely held views rather than just conflicts of interest.
We next ask why clients follow these recommendations. In the “money doctor” view of
Gennaioli, Shleifer, and Vishny (2015), investors delegate their portfolio decisions to advisors
they trust, and this trust reduces their anxiety about investing in risky assets, allowing them
to take more risk than they would on their own. We test two predictions of this view. First, if
trust builds up over time, equity shares should rise with the length of the advice relationship.
Indeed, retirees who have been advised for more than ten years hold about 7 percentage
points more equity than those in their first year, and this increase does not come with higher
fees. Second, advisors’ influence should be strongest for clients who are least confident in
making investment decisions on their own. Consistent with this prediction, the equity shares
of clients with low self-reported financial knowledge, and especially of those with low risk
tolerance, are more sensitive to those of their advisor’s other clients: the sensitivity for the
least risk-tolerant clients is twice as high as that for the most risk-tolerant clients.
Are these sincerely held beliefs justified, or are they misguided? Linnainmaa et al. (2021)
show that advisors hold misguided beliefs about active management: like many retail in-
vestors, they trade frequently, chase returns, and prefer expensive, actively managed funds.
To assess whether advisors’ beliefs about the appropriate level of equity exposure can be
rationalized as optimal or are similarly misguided, we turn to a standard life-cycle model of
consumption and portfolio choice.
In the model, retired households have constant relative risk aversion preferences and a
warm-glow bequest motive, face mortality risk, receive safe pension income, and pay invest-
ment fees calibrated to our data. We estimate risk aversion and the strength of the bequest
motive by matching the age profiles of equity shares in advised portfolios and of financial
wealth among Canadian retirees. With a moderate risk aversion of 4.2, the model closely
reproduces the high and gradually declining equity shares of advised retirees. Because the
typical retiree has modest financial wealth relative to safe pension income, which acts as a
4
large bond holding, a high equity share of financial wealth is optimal given the historical
equity premium. The portfolios of advised retirees can easily be rationalized by a standard
model: advisors’ beliefs about equity exposure thus appear justified rather than misguided.
We capture the money doctor mechanism in reduced form as a change in beliefs: advisors
bring their clients’ expectations closer to the true distribution of stock returns. We use the
model to quantify the value of advice through this channel. In a counterfactual without
advice, households hold pessimistic beliefs about stock returns, consistent with evidence
that beliefs shape household portfolios (Ameriks, K´ ezdi, Lee, and Shapiro, 2020; Giglio,
Maggiori, Stroebel, and Utkus, 2021; Meeuwis, Parker, Schoar, and Simester, 2022), and
invest in low-cost funds without advisor compensation. We calibrate these beliefs to match
the lower equity shares of non-advised retirees, which requires a perceived equity premium
of 2.4 percent, about 40 percent of the historical premium. Relative to this counterfactual,
advice raises both the level and the volatility of retirees’ consumption. We compute the
additional annual investment fee that advised households could pay and still be as well off
as without advice. We evaluate households without advice in two ways: by the welfare they
actually achieve under the true return distribution, and by the welfare they anticipate given
their pessimistic beliefs. Under the first, objective measure, the higher risk-taking induced
by advice is worth 70 basis points per year. Under the second, subjective measure, which
also counts the gain in perceived welfare from correcting pessimistic beliefs, the value of
advice more than doubles to 160 basis points per year. The implied cost of advice in our
data, 140 basis points per year, lies between these two estimates.
A natural concern with this counterfactual is that advised and non-advised retirees may
differ in their preferences. If retirees who seek advice are more willing to take financial risk,
part of the gap would exist even without advice, and our welfare estimates would overstate
the benefits of advice. However, attributing the entire gap to preferences would require a risk
aversion coefficient of 9.3 for non-advised retirees, more than twice our estimate for advised
retirees. This difference is more than five times the cross-sectional standard deviation of risk
5
aversion estimated by Calvet, Campbell, Gomes, and Sodini (2026). Moreover, most advised
retirees report only moderate risk tolerance, and those with the lowest risk tolerance follow
their advisors most closely. Selection could even go the other way: in the money doctor
model, the most anxious investors are the ones who seek advice. Finally, the gap is similar
relative to the glide path of the largest Canadian target-date fund family, which reflects a
prescription rather than investors’ choice; calibrating the counterfactual to this glide path
yields comparable welfare gains.
Our paper contributes to three strands of literature. First, we contribute to the literature
on household portfolio choice over the life cycle and in retirement (see Gomes, 2020; Gomes,
Haliassos, and Ramadorai, 2021, for reviews). Empirical studies document how equity shares
vary with age (e.g., Ameriks and Zeldes, 2004; Fagereng et al., 2017; Parker, Schoar, Cole,
and Simester, 2025), and a growing literature studies how retirees draw down their wealth
(Poterba, Venti, and Wise, 2011; Brown, Poterba, and Richardson, 2017, 2022; French, Jones,
and McGee, 2023). To match the modest equity shares observed in household data, life-
cycle models typically require high risk aversion or substantial background risk (Fagereng
et al., 2017; Catherine, 2022), although low equity shares may also reflect participation
frictions (Choukhmane and de Silva, 2026). We show that advised retirees’ portfolios look
very different, with high equity shares that a standard life-cycle model rationalizes with
moderate risk aversion. Given the prevalence of advice at older ages, our results highlight
the importance of accounting for financial advisors when studying retirees’ portfolio choices.
Although we rely on Canadian data, the decumulation problem is similar in other DC-
dominated countries. Like U.S. IRAs, the Registered Retirement Income Funds (RRIFs) in
our data require mandatory minimum withdrawals, and retirees combine individual account-
based savings with public and employer pensions.
Second, we contribute to the literature on target-date funds and default investment op-
tions in retirement plans. Target-date funds, which automatically reduce equity exposure
with age, have become a dominant investment vehicle since the Pension Protection Act of
6
2006 designated them as qualified default investment alternatives, a role reinforced by em-
ployees’ tendency to stick with defaults (Madrian and Shea, 2001). 5 Recent studies have
questioned whether their glide paths are optimal for retirees (Anarkulova, Cederburg, and
O’Doherty, 2025; Duarte, Fonseca, Goodman, and Parker, 2026). We show that advised
retirees hold about 35 percentage points more equity than the glide path of the largest
Canadian target-date fund family, and our model suggests that this higher risk-taking can
raise retirees’ expected consumption and welfare. For retirees with substantial safe pen-
sion income, target-date glide paths may therefore be too conservative. Our findings have
implications for retirees’ welfare and for the design of these funds.
Third, we contribute to the literature on the costs and benefits of financial advice (e.g.,
Bergstresser, Chalmers, and Tufano, 2009; Hackethal, Haliassos, and Jappelli, 2012; Mul-
lainathan, Noeth, and Schoar, 2012; von Gaudecker, 2015; Kim, Maurer, and Mitchell, 2016).
Much of this literature finds that advice is costly and potentially conflicted: advised portfo-
lios lag passive benchmarks (Foerster et al., 2017) and deliver lower Sharpe ratios (Chalmers
and Reuter, 2020), and misconduct is common (Egan et al., 2019). We extend these studies
in three ways. We first investigate how advisors shape risk-taking in retirement, a stage of the
life cycle that has received little attention in this literature and in which previous results on
advisor influence need not hold. We then compare advised portfolios with the predictions of
a standard life-cycle model. In contrast to advisors’ misguided views on active management
(Linnainmaa et al., 2021), their views on the appropriate level of risk-taking can easily be ra-
tionalized by the model. Our counterfactual analysis shows that the value of advice through
this channel is of the same order of magnitude as advisory fees. Finally, we provide evidence
consistent with a trust mechanism, supporting the money doctor model of Gennaioli et al.
(2015) and complementing prior work on the importance of trust in advisory relationships
(Kostovetsky, 2016; Gurun, Stoffman, and Yonker, 2018, 2021; Germann, Mertes, Weber,
and Loos, 2025). More broadly, our results complement findings that advisors provide valu-
5In 2021, the assets invested in these funds reached almost $6 trillion, or about 22% of all the assets
invested in U.S. mutual funds (Parker, Schoar, and Sun, 2023).
7
able non-alpha services such as financial planning (Previtero and Xing, 2025) and increase
stock market participation (Linnainmaa et al., 2025). Our findings also inform the global
debate over banning commissions in financial advice: such bans may reduce access to advice,
and we quantify a benefit of advice—advisors facilitate retirees’ risk-taking—that should be
weighed against its costs.
1 Data
1.1 Survey Data from Canadian Financial Monitor
We start by documenting differences in portfolio allocations between advised and non-advised
Canadian households in survey data. We use data from the Canadian Financial Monitor
(CFM), a household survey administered by the market research firm Ipsos-Reid. The CFM
collects detailed information on households’ personal banking relationships, investment hold-
ings, credit use, insurance products, and—crucially for our purposes—whether households
rely on financial advice. The survey is conducted at a monthly frequency and consists of
repeated cross-sections of approximately 1,000 households per month. We use data from
January 1999, the inception of the survey, through December 2006. We apply the survey
weights provided by the CFM to construct nationally representative estimates.
Our analysis focuses on Canadian households that hold an investment account. We
therefore restrict the sample to households with a positive balance in an account other than
checking or savings accounts. We further limit the sample to households with heads aged
25 to 85. We define retirees as households with a head aged 65 or older who reports being
retired.
The CFM contains a series of yes-or-no questions that ask households whether they
received free or paid advice on various aspects of their financial situation, including their
retirement plan, overall financial plan, insurance, estate planning, and tax planning. We
classify households as receiving paid investment advice if they report receiving paid advice
8
on either their retirement plan or their overall financial plan. Households are classified as
receiving free investment advice if they report receiving free advice on one of these two
categories but no paid advice. Households that report neither free nor paid advice on their
retirement plan or overall financial plan are classified as unadvised.
Table 1 reports summary statistics on asset allocations and financial characteristics by
advice status, both for the full sample of investors and for the subsample of retirees. Portfolio
allocations differ markedly across advice groups. Among all investors, the average equity
share is 57 percent for households receiving paid advice, compared to 36 percent for unadvised
households. Differences are even more pronounced among retirees: retirees with paid advice
hold, on average, 49 percent of their financial portfolios in equities, whereas unadvised
retirees hold only 24 percent. Households receiving free advice exhibit only slightly higher
equity exposure than unadvised households.
Two additional patterns are noteworthy. First, the equity shares of unadvised households
are similar to those documented in prior studies of household portfolio choice in other coun-
tries (e.g., Gomes and Michaelides, 2005; Fagereng et al., 2017). Second, equity exposure
among advised retirees is only modestly lower than that of advised investors overall, suggest-
ing that higher equity allocations persist well into retirement among households receiving
professional advice.
Taken together, these summary statistics suggest that financial advisors may exert a
substantial influence on household portfolio risk-taking, including among retired households,
which are the focus of our analysis. At the same time, the survey evidence has important
limitations: the numbe

In addition to the level of risk aversion, two other features of the baseline model help
explain the relatively high equity share it generates compared with models in the literature
that are calibrated or estimated to match conditional equity shares in non-advised portfolios.
First, the model features an equity Sharpe ratio directly taken from the data, which is higher
than values typically used in the literature. Specifically, while many studies calibrate the
annual equity premium to roughly 4% (with an equity return volatility around 18%, similar
to our parameterization), we use an equity premium of 5.7%, consistent with historically
realized returns in Canada. The resulting higher Sharpe ratio naturally increases the optimal
equity share in the model.
Second, the model matches the empirically observed wealth accumulation profile, which
features relatively low levels of financial wealth even around retirement. Median financial
wealth starts around C $100 thousand at age 65, less than four times the typical pension
income. Figure 9a illustrates the distribution of normalized cash on hand in the model,
32
and Figure 9b plots the corresponding policy function for the optimal equity share as a
function of normalized cash on hand. For a given age, the optimal equity share decreases
with the level of financial wealth, holding pension income fixed. Figure 9c shows that for a
typical retiree with normalized cash on hand between 5 and 10, consumption approximately
equals pension income. Because a large share of retirees’ remaining lifetime consumption
is financed by pension income in the form of a safe annuity, households optimally invest
the residual component of their overall wealth—financial wealth—more aggressively in risky
assets. Once we account for the composition of household balance sheets, the model-implied
portfolio allocations closely align with the data.
Finally, it is worth noting that, by adopting a fairly standard life-cycle model, we have
abstracted from some aspects of the saving and investment problem that are particularly
relevant for retirees. While the model incorporates uncertainty over the remaining lifetime
and a bequest motive—features that the literature has emphasized as key for understanding
saving behavior at older ages (e.g., De Nardi et al., 2010; Horneff, Maurer, Mitchell, and
Stamos, 2010; Ameriks et al., 2011; Inkmann, Lopes, and Michaelides, 2011)—it abstracts
from health and medical expenditure risk. Analogous to idiosyncratic labor income risk
as the main source of background risk during the working life, health shocks represent an
important form of idiosyncratic risk in retirement (Hubbard, Skinner, and Zeldes, 1994;
Horneff, Maurer, Mitchell, and Stamos, 2009; De Nardi et al., 2010; Ameriks et al., 2011). For
a careful treatment of the implications of health risks on retirees’ portfolio choice, see Yogo
(2016). Because background risks increase households’ effective risk aversion, introducing
additional sources of risk would lead to a lower estimate of γ to rationalize the same high
equity shares observed in the data. Since a moderately lower estimate of risk aversion would
still lie within the range of values typically considered reasonable, incorporating additional
background risks is unlikely to alter our main conclusions.
33
4.3 Counterfactual: Reduced Risk-Taking
While our empirical findings are consistent with the predictions of a standard life-cycle model,
the portfolio allocations of advised retirees differ strikingly from those of non-advised retirees,
from conventional investment advice—such as the “100 − age” rule—and from the glide
paths implemented by common target-date funds. To assess the quantitative implications of
these differences, we consider a counterfactual scenario in which households without financial
advisors optimally choose substantially lower equity shares in retirement.
To rationalize why unadvised households may optimally hold substantially less risky
portfolios, we build on the “money doctors” hypothesis of Gennaioli et al. (2015). The central
idea is that financial advice primarily influences households by shaping their beliefs about the
distribution of future asset returns. In the absence of professional advice, households may
hold pessimistic expectations about equity returns, leading them to underinvest in risky
assets. Financial advisors act as money doctors by correcting these distorted beliefs and
aligning clients’ expectations with the objective return distribution, which in turn induces
higher equity exposure.
We operationalize this mechanism by modeling a belief distortion: in the no-advice coun-
terfactual, households’ subjective expectations of the equity premium are tilted downward
relative to the true distribution. In contrast, when paired with an advisor—as in our baseline
model—households hold rational beliefs about the equity premium. The difference in equity
allocations between advised and unadvised portfolios can then be interpreted as the conse-
quence of advisors bringing clients’ expectations about equity returns closer to the objective
distribution.
Formally, unadvised households perceive the expected equity return to be lower than the

4.4 Welfare-Equivalent Investment Fees
To quantify the economic value of financial advice in our setting, we use the counterfactual
described in Section 4.3 and translate welfare differences between the advised baseline econ-
omy and the no-advice counterfactual into an equivalent annual portfolio management fee.
Specifically, we ask what additional annual fee, charged on both equity and bond holdings,
advised households could pay and still be as well off as in the counterfactual without advice.
Because higher fees reduce lifetime utility, a larger welfare-equivalent fee implies a greater
welfare gain from financial advice.
36
We consider two distinct welfare concepts. In both, welfare in the advised economy is
computed under the true data-generating process for returns, which is also what advised
households believe. The two concepts differ only in how we evaluate households without
advice. In the first, objective evaluation, welfare in the no-advice counterfactual is also
computed under the true process. This measures the expected lifetime utility that households
without advice actually achieve, given their overly conservative choices. In the second,
subjective evaluation, welfare in the no-advice counterfactual is computed using households’
own pessimistic beliefs about returns. This measures the (lower) expected lifetime utility
these households anticipate. The difference between the two measures captures the increase
in subjective welfare from correcting pessimistic beliefs, beyond their effects on consumption
and portfolio choices. This component is close in spirit to the “money doctor” view of
Gennaioli et al. (2015), in which households value advice not only because it improves their
portfolios but also because it changes how they feel about investing.
Figure 11 reports the resulting welfare-equivalent equity fees under both perspectives. In
the no-advice counterfactual, households pay an annual fee of 1.1% on equity funds. Under
the objective evaluation, the equity fee at which advised households are as well off as house-
holds without advice is 1.8%. In other words, the welfare gain from advice—from overcoming
the overly conservative choices driven by pessimistic beliefs—is worth an incremental fee of
70 basis points per year.
Under the subjective evaluation, the value of advice is even larger: the equity fee for
advised portfolios would have to rise to 2.7% to make households indifferent to paying 1.1%
in the no-advice counterfactual. The reason is that, from households’ subjective perspective,
advice delivers two distinct benefits. First, it leads households to make less conservative
choices, which raises expected lifetime utility under the true return distribution. This is
the 70-basis-point gain captured by the objective evaluation. Second, it eliminates the
pessimistic beliefs about future returns that cause households to fear lower future wealth and
consumption, thereby directly increasing perceived welfare. This accounts for the remaining
37
90 basis points of the increased fee. Thus, counting the gain in perceived welfare from
more accurate, less pessimistic expectations about the future more than doubles the value
of advice.
These estimates are of the same order of magnitude as the implied cost of advice in our
data, 1.4% per year. The objective welfare gain from higher risk-taking alone covers about
half of this cost, and including the gain in perceived welfare brings the value of advice slightly
above it. The fact that households’ subjective valuation of advice exceeds its objective welfare
benefits is consistent with the “money doctor” view. Our analysis abstracts from other
potential sources of value added by financial advisors—such as help with financial planning
or implementing tax-efficient strategies—which would further increase both measures.
Conclusion
More Americans are turning 65 than at any time in history, more than four million per year
through 2027 (Fichtner, 2024). With the shift from defined benefit to defined contribution
plans, many of these retirees must decide how to invest their savings throughout retirement,
a complex problem at an age when cognitive abilities decline. Financial advisors can help
retirees navigate these decisions. Do they?
To address this question, we study the portfolios of more than 36,000 advised Canadian
retirees. Advised retirees keep about two-thirds of their portfolios in equities well into old
age, 30 to 40 percentage points more than non-advised retirees, target-date funds, or common
rules of thumb. Advisors have a strong impact on these allocations. Because advisors hold
similarly high equity shares in their own portfolios, even after they stop advising clients,
these high equity allocations are likely to reflect advisors’ genuine beliefs rather than just
conflicts of interest. Instead, the evidence is consistent with trust playing a central role:
advisors’ influence grows with client tenure, and it is strongest among clients with low risk
tolerance and limited financial knowledge.
38
A standard life-cycle model with moderate risk aversion can easily rationalize these high
equity shares, because retirees’ financial wealth is modest relative to their safe pension
income. If advisors raise risk-taking by correcting their clients’ pessimistic beliefs about
stock returns, the welfare gains from advice are worth up to 160 basis points per year. Of
these, 70 basis points come from higher risk-taking, and 90 more come from more accurate,
less pessimistic expectations about the future. This second component is not an objective
welfare gain: it reflects instead how advice changes the way households feel about investing,
as in the “money doctor” view (Gennaioli et al., 2015). These values are of the same order
of magnitude as the cost of advice.
Our findings have several broader implications. First, evaluations of financial advice
typically focus on fees and risk-adjusted performance. Our results suggest that advisors’
influence on the level of risk-taking is an important source of value, particularly for retirees.
Second, for retirees with substantial safe pension income, the traditional glide paths of
target-date funds may be too conservative. Third, the aging of the population may have
consequences for aggregate financial markets (e.g., Poterba, 2001), and Parker et al. (2023)
show that the growth of target-date funds has changed the dynamics of stock prices. The
aggregate demand for equities as the population ages may therefore depend on the extent
to which retirees invest through target-date funds or with financial advisors. Understanding
these aggregate consequences is an important direction for future research.
